entries.7ff2b2958cc05ec6a097658c4de06b566aa73dc9: <div sID="gen13123" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="138" osisID="Ps.138" sID="Ps.138"/> <div eID="gen13123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13124" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13125" type="x-p"/> It does not appear, nor is it material to enquire, upon what occasion David penned this psalm; but in it, I. He looks back with thankfulness upon the experiences he had had of God's goodness to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.138.1-Ps.138.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. He looks forward with comfort, in hopes, 1. That others would go on to praise God like him, <reference osisRef="Ps.138.4-Ps.138.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. 2. That God would go on to do good to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.138.6-Ps.138.8">ver. 6-8</reference>. In singing this psalm we must in like manner devote ourselves to God's praise and glory and repose ourselves in his power and goodness.
entries.754dbe15b15583f8b2dee560e68394936c86d33d: <div eID="gen13125" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13124" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Grateful Praise.</title> <div sID="gen13126" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I will praise thee with my whole heart: before the gods will I sing praise unto thee. <hi type="super">2</hi> I will worship toward thy holy temple, and praise thy name for thy lovingkindness and for thy truth: for thou hast magnified thy word above all thy name. <hi type="super">3</hi> In the day when I cried thou answeredst me, <hi type="italic">and</hi> strengthenedst me <hi type="italic">with</hi> strength in my soul. 4 All the kings of the earth shall praise thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , when they hear the words of thy mouth. 5 Yea, they shall sing in the ways of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for great <hi type="italic">is</hi> the glory of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen13126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13127" type="x-p"/> I. How he would praise God, compare <reference osisRef="Ps.111.1">Ps. cxi. 1</reference>. 1. He will praise him with sincerity and zeal—"<hi type="italic">With my heart, with my whole heart,</hi> with that which is within me and with all that is within me, with uprightness of intention and fervency of affection, inward impressions agreeing with outward expressions." 2. With freedom and boldness: <hi type="italic">Before the gods will I sing praise unto thee,</hi> before the princes, and judges, and great men, either those of other nations that visited him or those of his own nation that attended on him, even in their presence. He will not only praise God with his heart, which we may do by pious ejaculations in any company, but will sing praise if there be occasion. Note, Praising God is work which the greatest of men need not be ashamed of; it is the work of angels, the work of heaven. <hi type="italic">Before the angels</hi> (so some understand it), that is, in religious assemblies, where there is a special presence of angels, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.10">1 Cor. xi. 10</reference>. 3. In the way that God had appointed: <hi type="italic">I will worship towards thy holy temple.</hi> The priests alone went into the temple; the people, at the nearest, did but worship towards it, and that they might do at a distance. Christ is our temple, and towards him we must look with an eye of faith, as Mediator between us and God, in all our praises of him. Heaven is God's holy temple, and thitherward we must lift up our eyes in all our addresses to God. <hi type="italic">Our Father in heaven.</hi> <div eID="gen13127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13128" type="x-p"/> II. What he would praise God for. 1. For the fountain of his comforts—<hi type="italic">for thy lovingkindness and for thy truth,</hi> for thy goodness and for thy promise, mercy hidden in thee and mercy revealed by thee, that God is a gracious God in himself and has engaged to be so to all those that trust in him. <hi type="italic">For thou hast magnified thy word</hi> (thy promise, which is truth) <hi type="italic">above all thy name.</hi> God has made himself known to us in many ways in creation and providence, but most clearly by his word. The judgments of his mouth are magnified even above those of his hand, and greater things are done by them. The wonders of grace exceed the wonders of nature; and what is discovered of God by revelation is much greater than what is discovered by reason. In what God had done for David his faithfulness to his work appeared more illustriously, and redounded more to his glory, than any other of his attributes. Some good interpreters understand it of Christ, the essential Word, and of his gospel, which are magnified above all the discoveries God had before made of himself to the fathers. He that magnified the law, and made that honourable, magnifies the gospel much more. 2. For the streams flowing from that fountain, in which he himself had tasted that the Lord is gracious, <reference osisRef="Ps.138.3">v. 3</reference>. He had been in affliction, and he remembers, with thankfulness, (1.) The sweet communion he then had with God. He cried, he prayed, and prayed earnestly, and God answered him, gave him to understand that his prayer was accepted and should have a gracious return in due time. The intercourse between God and his saints is carried on by his promises and their prayers. (2.) The sweet communications he then had from God: <hi type="italic">Thou strengthenedst me with strength in my soul.</hi> This was the answer to his prayer, for God gives more than good words, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.6">Ps. xx. 6</reference>. Observe, [1.] It was a speedy answer: <hi type="italic">In the day when I cried.</hi> Note, Those that trade with heaven by prayer grow rich by quick returns. <hi type="italic">While we are yet speaking God hears,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.65.24">Isa. lxv. 24</reference>. [2.] It was a spiritual answer. God gave him strength in his soul, and that is a real and valuable answer to the prayer of faith in the day of affliction. If God give us strength in our souls to bear the burdens, resist the temptations, and do the duties of an afflicted state, if he strengthen us to keep hold of himself by faith, to maintain the peace of our own minds and to wait with patience for the issue, we must own that he has answered us, and we are bound to be thankful. <div eID="gen13128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13129" type="x-p"/> III. What influence he hoped that his praising God would have upon others, <reference osisRef="Ps.138.4-Ps.138.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. David was himself a king, and therefore he hoped that kings would be wrought upon by his experiences, and his example, to embrace religion; and, if kings became religious, their kingdoms would be every way better. Now, 1. This may have reference to the kings that were neighbours to David, as Hiram and others. "They shall all praise thee." When they visited David, and, after his death, when they sought the presence of Solomon (as <hi type="italic">all the kings of the earth</hi> are expressly said to have done, <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.23">2 Chron. ix. 23</reference>), they readily joined in the worship of the God of Israel. 2. It may look further, to the calling of the Gentiles and the discipling of all nations by the gospel of Christ, of whom it is said that <hi type="italic">all kings shall fall down before him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.72.11">Ps. lxxii. 11</reference>. Now it is here foretold, (1.) That <hi type="italic">the kings of the earth shall hear the words of God.</hi> All that came near David should hear them from him, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.46">Ps. cxix. 46</reference>. In the latter days the preachers of the gospel should be sent into all the world. (2.) That then they shall praise God, as all those have reason to do that hear his word, and receive it in the light and love of it, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.48">Acts xiii. 48</reference>. (3.) That they shall <hi type="italic">sing in the ways of the Lord,</hi> in the ways of his providence and grace towards them; they shall rejoice in God, and give glory to him, however he is pleased to deal with them in the ways of their duty and obedience to him. Note, Those that walk in the ways of the Lord have reason to sing in those ways, to go on in them with a great deal of cheerfulness, for they are ways of pleasantness, and it becomes us to be pleasant in them; and, if we are so, <hi type="italic">great is the glory of the Lord.</hi> It is very much for the honour of God that kings should walk in his ways, and that all those who walk in them should sing in them, and so proclaim to all the world that he is a good Master and his work its own wages.
entries.24177c2091934b2707ce97deb412a4aacc8d410d: <div eID="gen13129" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Care of His People.</title> <div sID="gen13130" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Though the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">be</hi> high, yet hath he respect unto the lowly: but the proud he knoweth afar off. <hi type="super">7</hi> Though I walk in the midst of trouble, thou wilt revive me: thou shalt stretch forth thine hand against the wrath of mine enemies, and thy right hand shall save me. <hi type="super">8</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will perfect <hi type="italic">that which</hi> concerneth me: thy mercy, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever: forsake not the works of thine own hands. <div eID="gen13130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13131" type="x-p"/> David here comforts himself with three things:— <div eID="gen13131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13132" type="x-p"/> I. The favour God bears to his humble people (<reference osisRef="Ps.138.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Though the Lord be high,</hi> and neither needs any of his creatures nor can be benefited by them, <hi type="italic">yet has he respect unto the lowly,</hi> smiles upon them as well pleased with them, overlooks heaven and earth to cast a gracious look upon them (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa. lvii. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.1">lxvi. 1</reference>), and, sooner or later, he will put honour upon them, while <hi type="italic">he knows the proud afar off,</hi> knows them, but disowns them and rejects them, how proudly soever they pretend to his favour. Dr. Hammond makes this to be the sum of that gospel which the kings of the earth shall hear and welcome—that penitent sinners shall be accepted of God, but the impenitent cast out; witness the instance of the Pharisee and the publican, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.9-Luke.18.14">Luke xviii.</reference> <div eID="gen13132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13133" type="x-p"/> II. The care God takes of his afflicted oppressed people, <reference osisRef="Ps.138.7">v. 7</reference>. David, though a great and good man, expects to <hi type="italic">walk in the midst of trouble,</hi> but encourages himself with hope, 1. That God would comfort him: "When my spirit is ready to sink and fail, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> shalt <hi type="italic">revive me,</hi> and make me easy and cheerful under my troubles." Divine consolations have enough in them to revive us even when we walk in the midst of troubles and are ready to die away for fear. 2. That he would protect him, and plead his cause: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt stretch forth thy hand,</hi> though not against my enemies to destroy them, yet <hi type="italic">against the wrath of my enemies,</hi> to restrain that and set bounds to it." 3. That he would in due time work deliverance for him: <hi type="italic">Thy right hand shall save me.</hi> As he has one hand to stretch out against his enemies, so he has another to save his own people. Christ is the right hand of the Lord, that shall save all those who serve him. <div eID="gen13133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13134" type="x-p"/> III. The assurance we have that whatever good work God has begun in and for his people he will perform it (<reference osisRef="Ps.138.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord will perfect that which concerns me,</hi> 1. That which is most needful for me; and he knows best what is so. We <hi type="italic">are careful and cumbered about many things</hi> that do not concern us, but he knows what are the things that really are of consequence to us (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.32">Matt. vi. 32</reference>) and he will order them for the best. 2. That which we are most concerned about. Every good man is most concerned about his duty to God and his happiness in God, that the former may be faithfully done and the latter effectually secured; and if indeed these are the things that our hearts are most upon, and concerning which we are most solicitous, there is a good work begun in us, and he that has begun it will perfect it, we may be confident he will, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.6">Phil. i. 6</reference>. Observe, (1.) What ground the psalmist builds this confidence upon: <hi type="italic">Thy mercy, O Lord! endures for ever.</hi> This he had made very much the matter of his praise (<reference osisRef="Ps.13.6">Ps. xiii. 6</reference>), and therefore he could here with the more assurance make it the matter of his hope. For, if we give God the glory of his mercy, we may take to ourselves the comfort of it. Our hopes that we shall persevere must be founded, not upon our own strength, for that will fail us, but upon the mercy of God, for that will not fail. It is well pleaded, "<hi type="italic">Lord, thy mercy endures for ever;</hi> let me be for ever a monument of it." (2.) What use he makes of this confidence; it does not supersede, but quicken prayer; he turns his expectation into a petition: "<hi type="italic">Forsake not,</hi> do not let go, <hi type="italic">the work of thy own hands.</hi> Lord, I am the work of thy own hands, my soul is so, do not forsake me; my concerns are so, do not lay by thy care of them." Whatever good there is in us it is the work of God's own hands; <hi type="italic">he works in us both to will and to do;</hi> it will fail if he forsake it; but his glory, as Jehovah, a perfecting God, is so much concerned in the progress of it to the end that we may in faith pray, "Lord, do not forsake it." Whom he loves he loves to the end; and, as for God, his work is perfect.  <chapter eID="Ps.138"/> <div eID="gen13134" type="x-p"/>

entries.ab93f7c2ee650cee9fd1574ae549c6156749aa46: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7078"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 138</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.138.1-Ps.138.8">Psa 138:1-8</reference>. David thanks God for His benefits, and anticipating a wider extension of God's glory by His means, assures himself of His continued presence and faithfulness.</title> <div sID="gen10854" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7078"/><hi type="bold">1. I will praise thee with my whole heart--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.9.1">Psa 9:1</reference>).<div eID="gen10854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10855" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before the gods--</hi>whether angels (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.5">Psa 8:5</reference>); or princes (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.6">Ex 21:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.82.6">Psa 82:6</reference>); or idols (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.7">Psa 97:7</reference>); denotes a readiness to worship the true God alone, and a contempt of all other objects of worship. <div eID="gen10855" type="x-p"/>
entries.cfa1d1ad3be8e4d36177eda3947b0d5ab86b9c87: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7079"/><div sID="gen10856" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7079"/>2. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.5.7">Psa 5:7</reference>).<div eID="gen10856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10857" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy word above all thy name--</hi>that is, God's promise (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.12-2Sam.7.16">2Sa 7:12-16</reference>), sustained by His mercy and truth, exceeded all other manifestations of Himself as subject of praise. <div eID="gen10857" type="x-p"/>
entries.2aa899109b9849d64da90d3e248f08da0c1b6e2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7080"/><div sID="gen10858" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7080"/>3-5. That promise, as an answer to his prayers in distress, revived and strengthened his faith; and, as the basis of other revelations of the Messiah, it will be the occasion of praise by all who hear and receive it (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.29">Psa 68:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.31">31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.4.3">Is 4:3</reference>). <div eID="gen10858" type="x-p"/>
entries.9584074a1c4df0a2fe8ba81973b5e74b7553bed1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7082"/><div sID="gen10860" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7082"/>6-7. On this general principle of God's government (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">Is 2:11</reference>; 57:15; 66:2), he relies for God's favor in saving him, and overthrowing his enemies.<div eID="gen10860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knoweth afar off--</hi>their ways and deserts (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Psa 1:6</reference>). <div eID="gen10861" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f4c72904e2779a48901560bc5e8bebc806fda6a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7083"/><div sID="gen10862" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7083"/>8. God will fulfil His promise. <chapter eID="Ps.138"/>

entries.cc5f5428e9087a7ec2075a2ef67a83a0501b498d: <div eID="gen23291" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23292" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23293" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23293" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23292" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23294" type="x-p"/> The psalmist praises the Lord for his mercies to himself, <reference osisRef="Psa.138.1-Psa.138.3">Psa 138:1-3</reference>. He foretells that the kings of the earth shall worship him, <reference osisRef="Psa.138.4">Psa 138:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.138.5">Psa 138:5</reference>. God's condescension to the humble, <reference osisRef="Psa.138.6">Psa 138:6</reference>. The psalmist's confidence, <reference osisRef="Psa.138.7">Psa 138:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.138.8">Psa 138:8</reference>. <div eID="gen23294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23295" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew and all the Versions attribute this Psalm to David, and it is supposed to have been made by him when, delivered from all his enemies, he was firmly seated on the throne of Israel. As the Septuagint and Arabic prefix also the names of Haggai and Zechariah, it is probable that it was used by the Jews as a form of thanksgiving for their deliverance from all their enemies, and their ultimate settlement in their own land, after Ahasuerus, supposed by Calmet to be Darius Hystaspes, had married Esther, before which time they were not peaceably settled in their own country. <div eID="gen23295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23296" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23297" type="x-p"/> I will praise thee with my whole heart - I have received the highest favors from thee, and my whole soul should acknowledge my obligation to thy mercy. The Versions and several MSS. add יהוה Yehovah, "I will praise thee, O Lord," etc. <div eID="gen23297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23298" type="x-p"/> Before the gods will I sing - נגד אלהים neged Elohim, "in the presence of Elohim;" most probably meaning before the ark, where were the sacred symbols of the Supreme Being. The Chaldee has, before the judges. The Vulgate, before the angels. So the Septuagint, Ethiopic, Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon. The Syriac, Before kings will I sing unto thee. This place has been alleged by the Roman Catholics as a proof that the holy angels, who are present in the assemblies of God's people, take their prayers and praises, and present them before God. There is nothing like this in the text; for supposing, which is not granted, that the word elohim here signifies angels, the praises are not presented to them, nor are they requested to present them before God; it is simply said, Before elohim will I sing praise unto Thee. Nor could there be need of any intermediate agents, when it was well known that God himself was present in the sanctuary, sitting between the cherubim. Therefore this opinion is wholly without support from this place.
entries.aad0b877198dea05a80f4c6c809421e20b108689: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23299" type="x-p"/> For thy loving-kindness - Thy tender mercy shown to me; and for the fulfillment of thy truth - the promises thou hast made. <div eID="gen23299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23300" type="x-p"/> Thou hast magnified thy word above all thy name - All the Versions read this sentence thus: "For thou hast magnified above all the name of thy holiness," or, "thy holy name." Thou hast proved that thou hast all power in heaven and in earth, and that thou art true in all thy words. And by giving the word of prophecy, and fulfilling those words, thou hast magnified thy holy name above all things - thou hast proved thyself to be ineffably great. The original is the following: כי הגדלת על כל שמך אמרתך ki higdalta al col shimcha, imrathecha, which I think might be thus translated: "For thou hast magnified thy name and thy word over all," or, "on every occasion." Kennicott reads, "He preferred faithfulness to his promise to the attribute of his power." I believe my own translation to be nearest the truth. There may be some corruption in this clause.
entries.bd903355e1818964a63a122af41d12314e8aa273: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23301" type="x-p"/> With strength in my soul - Thou hast endued my soul with many graces, blessings, and heavenly qualities.
entries.153ebfce5064655fdf598ecf9f8f07bfbc099738: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23302" type="x-p"/> All the kings of the earth - Of the land: all the neighboring nations, seeing what is done for us, and looking in vain to find that any human agency was employed in the work, will immediately see that it was thy hand; and consequently, by confessing that it was thou, will give praise to thy name.
entries.07daa68aa8dd139a33950af9c6e46173fe73a4bb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23303" type="x-p"/> They shall sing in the ways of the Lord - They shall admire thy conduct, and the wondrous workings of thy providence, if they should not even unite with thy people.
entries.ea0ab4bf335ef1396ece6acd4fc3fcaca36a7b71: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23304" type="x-p"/> Though the Lord be high - Infinitely great as God is, he regards even the lowest and most inconsiderable part of his creation; but the humble and afflicted man attracts his notice particularly. <div eID="gen23304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23305" type="x-p"/> But the proud he knoweth afar off - He beholds them at a distance, and has them in utter derision.
entries.0463cbf0db75d340b040bd569e86c8dc6a8f912b: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23306" type="x-p"/> Though I walk in the midst of trouble - I have had such experience of thy mercy, that let me fall into whatsoever trouble I may, yet I will trust in thee. Thou wilt quicken me, though I were ready to die; and thou wilt deliver me from the wrath of my enemies.
entries.4329291743fbf3c94e413e32d5af4b69c34480d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23307" type="x-p"/> The Lord will perfect - Whatever is farther necessary to be done, he will do it. <div eID="gen23307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23308" type="x-p"/> Forsake not the works of thine own hands - My body - my soul; thy work begun in my soul; thy work in behalf of Israel; thy work in the evangelization of the world; thy work in the salvation of mankind. Thou wilt not forsake these.  <chapter eID="Ps.138"/> <div eID="gen23308" type="x-p"/>

entries.6a51b35187ca68d4bab948c92508083d1d832da8: <div eID="gen10265" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Mediator and Perfecter</title> <div sID="gen10266" type="x-p"/> There will come a time when the praise of Jahve, which according to <reference osisRef="Ps.137.3">Psa 137:3</reference> was obliged to be dumb in the presence of the heathen, will, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.138.5">Psa 138:5</reference>, be sung by the kings of the heathen themselves. In the lxx <reference osisRef="Ps.137.1-Ps.137.9">Psa 137:1-9</reference> side by side with τῷ Δαυίδ also has the inscription Ἱιερεμίου, and <reference osisRef="Ps.138.1-Ps.138.8">Psa 138:1-8</reference> has Ἀγγαίου καὶ Ζαχαρίου. Perhaps these statements are meant to refer back the existing recension of the text of the respective Psalms to the prophets named (vid., Köhler, <hi type="italic">Haggai</hi>, S. 33). From the fact that these names of psalmodists added by the lxx do not come down beyond Malachi, it follows that the Psalm-collection in the mind of the lxx was made not later than in the time of Nehemiah. <div eID="gen10266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10267" type="x-p"/> The speaker in <reference osisRef="Ps.138.1-Ps.138.8">Psa 138:1-8</reference>, to follow the lofty expectation expressed in <reference osisRef="Ps.138.4">Psa 138:4</reference>, is himself a king, and according to the inscription, David. There is, however, nothing to favour his being the author; the Psalm is, in respect for the Davidic Psalms, composed as it were out of the soul of David - an echo of 2 Sam. 7 (1 Chr. 17). The superabundant promise which made the throne of David and of his seed an eternal throne is here gratefully glorified. The Psalm can at any rate be understood, if with Hengstenberg we suppose that it expresses the lofty self-consciousness to which David was raised after victorious battles, when he humbly ascribed the glory to God and resolved to build Him a Temple in place of the tent upon Zion.
entries.a2020ae8f76851426f4db5b7f9bdee32c744c2c1: <reference osisRef="Ps.138.1-Ps.138.2">Psa 138:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen10267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10268" type="x-p"/> The poet will give thanks to Him, whom he means without mentioning Him by name, for His mercy, i.e., His anticipating, condescending love, and for His truth, i.e., truthfulness and faithfulness, and more definitely for having magnified His promise (אמרה) above all His Name, i.e., that He has given a promise which infinitely surpasses everything by which He has hitherto established a name and memorial for Himself (על־כּל־שׁמך, with <hi type="italic">ō</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">ŏ</hi>, an anomaly that is noted by the Masora, vid., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Psalterium</hi>, p. 133). If the promise by the mouth of Nathan (2 Sam. 7) is meant, then we may compare 2Sa 7:21. גּדל, גּדול, גּדלּה are repeated in that promise and its echo coming from the heart of David so frequently, that this הגדּלתּ seems like a hint pointing to that history, which is one of the most important crises in the history of salvation. The expression נגד אלהים also becomes intelligible from this history. Ewald renders it: “in the presence of God!” which is surely meant to say: in the holy place (De Wette, Olshausen). But “before God will I sing praise to Thee (O God!)” - what a jumble! The lxx renders ἐναντίον ἀγγέλων, which is in itself admissible and full of meaning,<note placement="foot">Bellarmine: <hi type="italic">Scio me psallentem tibi ab angelis, qui tibi assistunt, videri et attendi et ideo ita considerate me geram in psallendo, ut qui intelligam, in quo theatro consistam</hi>.</note> but without coherence in the context of the Psalm, and also is to be rejected because it is on the whole very questionable whether the Old Testament language uses אלהים thus, without anything further to define it, in the sense of “angels.” It might be more readily rendered “in the presence of the gods,” viz., of the gods of the peoples (Hengstenberg, Hupfeld, and Hitzig); but in order to be understood of gods which are only seemingly such, it would require some addition. Whereas אלהים can without any addition denote the magisterial possessors of the dignity that is the type of the divine, as follows from <reference osisRef="Ps.82.1">Psa 82:1</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>) in spite of Knobel, Graf, and Hupfeld; and thus, too (cf. נגד מלכים in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.46">Psa 119:46</reference>), we understand it here, with Rashi, Aben-Ezra, Kimchi, Falminius, Bucer, Clericus, and others. What is meant are “the great who are in the earth,” <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.9">2Sa 7:9</reference>, with whom David, inasmuch as he became king from being a shepherd, is ranked, and above whom he has been lifted up by the promise of an eternal kingship. Before these earthly “gods” will David praise the God of the promise; they shall hear for their salutary confusion, for their willing rendering of homage, that God hath made him “the highest with respect to the kings of the earth” (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.28">Psa 89:28</reference>).
entries.94b06ed150fa5daefb4eb59810e4f0ac4b7788a4: <reference osisRef="Ps.138.3-Ps.138.6">Psa 138:3-6</reference> <div eID="gen10268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10269" type="x-p"/> There are two things for which the poet gives thanks to God: He has answered him in the days of trouble connected with his persecution by Saul and in all distresses; and by raising him to the throne, and granting him victory upon victory, and promising him the everlasting possession of the throne, He has filled him with a proud courage, so that lofty feeling has taken up its abode in his soul, which was formerly fearful about help. Just as רהב signifies impetuosity, vehemence, and then also a monster, so הרהיב signifies both to break in upon one violently and overpowerlingly (Sol 6:5; cf. Syriac <hi type="italic">arheb</hi>, Arabic <hi type="italic">arhaba</hi>, to terrify), and to make any one courageous, bold, and confident of victory. בּנפשׁי עז forms a corollary to the verb that is marked by <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi> or <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>: so that in my soul there was עז, i.e., power, viz., a consciousness of power (cf. Jdg 5:21). The thanksgiving, which he, the king of the promise, offers to God on account of this, will be transmitted to all the kings of the earth when they shall hear (שׁמעוּ in the sense of a <hi type="italic">fut. exactum</hi>) the words of His mouth, i.e., the divine אמרה, and they shall sing of (שׁיר with בּ, like דּבּר בּ in <reference osisRef="Ps.87.3">Psa 87:3</reference>, שׂיח בּ in <reference osisRef="Ps.105.2">Psa 105:2</reference> and frequently, הלּל בּ in <reference osisRef="Ps.44.9">Psa 44:9</reference>, הזכּיר בּ in <reference osisRef="Ps.20.8">Psa 20:8</reference>, and the like) the ways of the God of the history of salvation, they shall sing that great is the glory of Jahve. <reference osisRef="Ps.138.6">Psa 138:6</reference> tells us by what means He has so super-gloriously manifested Himself in His leadings of David. He has shown Himself to be the Exalted One who is His all-embracing rule does not leave the lowly (cf. David’s confessions in <reference osisRef="Ps.131.1">Psa 131:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.22">2Sa 6:22</reference>) unnoticed (<reference osisRef="Ps.113.6">Psa 113:6</reference>), but on the contrary makes him the especial object of His regard; and on the other hand even from afar (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.139.2">Psa 139:2</reference>) He sees through (ידע as in <reference osisRef="Ps.94.11">Psa 94:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.23">Jer 29:23</reference>) the lofty one who thinks himself unobserved and conducts himself as if he were answerable to no higher being (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.4">Psa 10:4</reference>). In correct texts וגבה has <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>, and ממרחק <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>. The form of the <hi type="italic">fut. Kal</hi> יידע is formed after the analogy of the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> forms ייליל in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.7">Isa 16:7</reference>, and frequently, and ייטיב in <reference osisRef="Job.24.21">Job 24:21</reference>; probably the word is intended to be all the more emphatic, inasmuch as the first radical, which disappears in ידע, is thus in a certain measure restored.<note placement="foot">The Greek imperfects with the double (syllabic and temporal) augment, as ἑώρων, ἀνέῳγον, are similar. <hi type="italic">Chajuǵ</hi> also regards the first <hi type="italic">Jod</hi> in these forms as the preformative and the second as the radical, whereas Abulwalîd, <hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. ch. xxvi. p. 170, explains the first as a prosthesis and the second as the preformative. According to the view of others, e.g., of Kimchi, יידע might be <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. weakened from יהדע (יהידיע), which, apart from the unsuitable meaning, assumes a change of consonants that is all the more inadmissible as ידע itself springs from ודע. Nor is it to be supposed that יידע is modified from יידע (Luzzatto, §197), because it is nowhere written יידע.</note>
entries.62538a1c2297cf454d80b6ca8e8c2da09f36df9f: <reference osisRef="Ps.138.7-Ps.138.8">Psa 138:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen10269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10270" type="x-p"/> Out of these experiences-so important for all mankind - of David, who has been exalted by passing through humiliation, there arise from him confident hopes concerning the future. The beginning of this strophe calls <reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Psa 23:4</reference> to mind. Though his way may lead through the midst of heart - oppressing trouble, Jahve will loose these bands of death and quicken him afresh (חיּה as in <reference osisRef="Ps.30.4">Psa 30:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.71.20">Psa 71:20</reference>, and frequently). Though his enemies may rage, Jahve will stretch forth His hand threateningly and tranquillizingly over their wrath, and His right hand will save him. ימינך is the subject according to <reference osisRef="Ps.139.10">Psa 139:10</reference> and other passages, and not (for why should it be supposed to be this?) <hi type="italic">accus. instrumenti</hi> (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.60.7">Psa 60:7</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Ps.138.8">Psa 138:8</reference> יגמר is intended just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.57.3">Psa 57:3</reference> : the word begun He will carry out, ἐπιτελεῖν (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.6">Phi 1:6</reference>); and בּעדי (according to its meaning, properly: covering me) is the same as עלי in that passage (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.13.6">Psa 13:6</reference>; 142:8). The pledge of this completion is Jahve’s everlasting mercy, which will not rest until the promise is become perfect truth and reality. Thus, therefore, He will not leave, forsake the works of His hands (vid., Psa 90:16.), i.e., as Hengstenberg correctly explains, everything that He has hitherto accomplished for David, from his deliverance out of the hands of Saul down to the bestowment of the promise - He will not let one of His works stand still, and least of all one that has been so gloriously begun. הרפּה (whence תּרף) signifies to slacken, to leave slack, i.e., leave uncarried out, to leave to itself, as in Neh 6:3. אל expresses a negation with a measure of inward excitement.  <chapter eID="Ps.138"/> <div eID="gen10270" type="x-p"/>

entries.9241ea3c432f5080d919d63f38dd03f5d58dca1a:
PSALM 138
In this Psalm David, in remembrance of the singular help which had always been vouchsafed him by God — the experience he had enjoyed of his faithfulness and goodness, takes occasion to stir himself up to gratitude; and from what he had known of the divine faithfulness, he anticipates a continuance of the same mercy. If dangers must be met, he confidently looks for a happy issue.
A Psalm of David.
Psalm 138:1-5
1. I will praise thee
Here “O Jehovah” is to be understood. Though it is not in the received Hebrew text, it was found in six copies examined by Dr. Kennicott, and in eight examined by De Rossi. The Septuagint, Arabic, Vulgate, and AEthiopic versions add” Jehovah” after the verb for “praise.” “The omission of the Divine name,” says Jebb, in his Translation of the Psalms, “in a passage like this, at the beginning of the Psalm, is altogether unexampled.”
with my whole heart, before the gods
By the Hebrew word אלהים, Elohim, translated gods, Calvin understands “angels” or “kings,” but particularly the former. It is however proper to observe that אלהים, Elohim, is one of the names applied to the Supreme Being in the sacred volume, and therefore some critics translate “before God,” which they explain as meaning “before the ark,” where were the sacred symbols of his presence. If after the Hebrew word for “before,” we should suppose “thee” to be understood, the reading would be “before thee, or in thy presence, O God! will I sing praise unto thee.”
will I sing psalms to thee. 2. I will worship thee towards the temple of thy holiness, and sing unto thy name for thy mercy and for thy truth; for thou hast magnified thy name above all things by thy word. 3. In the day when I cried to thee then thou answeredst me, and hast abundantly ministered strength to me in my soul. 4. Let all kings of the earth praise thee, O Jehovah! because they have heard the words of thy mouth. 5. And let theta sing in
Phillips observes that the force of ב, beth, seems to be that of concerning: — “‘The kings of the earth shall sing concerning the ways of the Lord,’ how that they are good and merciful.”
the walls of Jehovah, for great is the glory of Jehovah.
 
1. I will praise thee with my whole heart As David had been honored to receive distinguishing marks of the divine favor, he declares his resolution to show more than ordinary gratitude. This is exercise which degenerates and is degraded in the case of hypocrites to a mere sound of empty words, but he states that he would return thanks to God not with the lips only, but with sincerity of heart, for by the whole heart, as we have elsewhere seen, is meant a heart which is sincere and not double. The noun אלהים, Elohim, sometimes means angels, and sometimes kings, and either meaning will suit with the passage before us. The praise David speaks of is that which is of a public kind. The solemn assembly is, so to speak, a heavenly theater, graced by the presence of attending angels; and one reason why the cherubim overshadowed the Ark of the Covenant was to let God’s people know that the angels are present when they come to worship in the sanctuary. We might very properly apply what is said here to kings, on account of their eminence in rank, as in Psalm 107:32, “Praise ye the Lord in the assembly of the elders” — that is, as we should say, in an assembly of an honored and illustrious kind. But I prefer the former sense, and this because believers in drawing near to God are withdrawn from the world, and rise to heaven in the enjoyment of fellowship with angels, so that we find Paul enforcing his address to the Corinthians upon the necessity of decency and order, by requiring them to show some respect at least in their public religious assemblies to the angels. (1 Corinthians 11:10.) The same thing was represented by God long before, under the figure of the cherubim, thus giving his people a visible pledge of his presence.

                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> for me.</ns0:note> con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerneth me <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Will finish that great work of my deliverance and ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vancement, which he hath undertaken and carried on hither<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to.</ns0:note>: thy mercy, O LORD, <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">It is not inconstant and changeable, as mens affecti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons are, but everlasting. And this may be either a proof of the foregoing assertion, <ns0:hi>the Lord will perfect,</ns0:hi> &c. or an argu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment to enforce the following petition, therefore <ns0:hi>forsake not,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note>: forsake not <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>leave not,</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>do not desist from</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>give over.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> the works of thine own hands <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The work of my salvation which is thus far advanced, not by any humane help, but by thine own extraordinary power and providence, and therefore it is not for thine honour to desert it at last. This he calls <ns0:hi>works</ns0:hi> in regard of the many and various parts and actions which concurred to this work.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
